When you call something barnstorming, you mean it is thrillingly impressive, full of wild energy, and done with spectacular skill. It describes something — a performance, a speech, a sporting display — that sweeps people off their feet, leaves them buzzing with excitement, and feels almost larger than life.

Think of it as a supercharged version of words like excellent or brilliant, but with a very specific flavour: a barnstorming performance doesn't just succeed — it storms in, takes the audience by surprise and leaves them on their feet.

In 19th-century America, touring actors travelled from one small farming town to the next and performed in barns, because there were no theatres. They were called barnstormers. In the 1920s, daredevil pilots did the same with aeroplanes — landing in farm fields and thrilling crowds with loops, rolls and wing-walking. From these bold, crowd-pleasing performers came the adjective: anything barnstorming has that same daring, rousing, crowd-winning energy.

• "She gave a barnstorming speech that brought the whole hall to its feet."
  • "United produced a barnstorming second half, scoring three goals in twenty minutes."
  • "It was a barnstorming debut album — loud, confident and impossible to ignore."

It is most common in British English, especially in writing about sport, politics, music and theatre. It is always positive, and it suggests excitement and energy, not quiet competence.
Barnstorming = thrillingly energetic and impressive, in a way that wins a crowd over.
